identity.title: Can Neural Networks Achieve Optimal Computational-statistical Tradeoff? An Analysis on Single-Index Model

problem.claim: Whether gradient-trained neural networks can attain the optimal statistical–computational tradeoff for Gaussian single-index models.

gap.claim: It was unknown whether neural networks could achieve the sample complexity implied by the SQ lower bound.

contributions.claim: A unified polynomial-time gradient-based algorithm for training two-layer neural networks across multiple loss and activation functions.
An extension using weight perturbation for learning signals that are k-sparse with k=o(√d).
A corresponding SQ lower bound for the sparse setting, matched by the proposed method up to polylogarithmic factors.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors identify the weight perturbation technique as novel and present the framework as potentially applicable beyond this problem, including sparse tensor PCA.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their algorithm learns a feature representation strongly aligned with the unknown signal and uses Õ(d^(s⋆/2)∨d) samples, matching the SQ lower bound up to a polylogarithmic factor for all s⋆≥1.
For k-sparse signals with k=o(√d), the authors report an SQ lower bound of Õmega(k^s⋆), matched by their method up to a polylogarithmic factor.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper asks whether gradient-based neural-network training can achieve the optimal tradeoff for Gaussian single-index models.
Existing SQ results give a polynomial-time sample lower bound, but neural networks' ability to attain it was unresolved.
The authors propose a unified gradient-based two-layer-network algorithm adaptable to varied losses and activations.
They report signal-aligned representations and near-SQ-optimal sample complexity, then extend the approach to sparse signals via weight perturbation.
The sparse extension is paired with a corresponding SQ lower bound that the method reportedly matches up to logarithmic factors.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs an unresolved benchmark question with an explicit lower bound and then states the proposed method's complexity relative to that bound.

lessons.interpretation: This makes the target of the method and the meaning of the reported rate easy to evaluate from the abstract alone.
lessons.application: Frame a theory contribution by naming the open benchmark, stating the relevant lower bound, and directly comparing the proposed rate under the same regime.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when no meaningful lower bound or common complexity measure exists.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates the dense result from a sparse extension and identifies the additional technique used for sparsity.

lessons.interpretation: Explicitly connecting a structural assumption to a tailored mechanism helps distinguish the core method from its adaptation.
lessons.application: When extending a method to a structured regime, state the structural condition, the added mechanism, and the separate guarantee in sequence.
lessons.exception: Avoid this separation when the extension changes the problem so substantially that the guarantees are not comparable.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact losses, activations, optimization procedure, or conditions behind the reported guarantees.
It does not provide experimental results, proof details, constants, or the precise polylogarithmic factors.
The claimed alignment is not quantified in the abstract, and the proposed relevance to sparse tensor PCA is presented only as a suggestion.
